edges.description: Peritoneal inflammation produces a protein-rich, lymphocyte-predominant exudate with a low serum-ascites albumin gradient; the vascular and lymphatic steps are not characterized in the cited sources.
The granulomatous inflammation heals with fibrosis that binds bowel, omentum and mesentery together.
Systemic symptoms accompany the peritoneal infection; the cytokine steps are not described in the cited sources.
Chronic infection causes weight loss; intermediates are not described.
Peritoneal inflammation causes abdominal pain, the commonest symptom.
Serum CA-125 rises in peritoneal tuberculosis; the source of the antigen (inflamed peritoneum) is not established in the cited sources.
Mesenteric lymph nodes draining the infected peritoneum enlarge.
The exudate accumulates as ascites.
Accumulating ascites distends the abdomen, the presentation of the distension-dominant (wet) form.
Fibrinous septa can partition the exudate.
Fibrosis forms adhesions.
Adhesions obstruct the bowel; in a cohort treated without steroids, laparotomy for obstruction found extensive adhesions.
Matted bowel, omentum and mesentery are felt as an abdominal mass.
Cirrhosis raises the risk of tuberculous peritonitis; malnutrition and impaired T cell-dependent function are proposed but unproven intermediates.

nodes.description: Corticosteroids added to antituberculous therapy to reduce peritoneal inflammation and fibrosis and so prevent adhesions and obstruction. A meta-analysis of three poor-quality studies (one quasi-randomized, two retrospective) found fewer strictures and obstructions, but the evidence is too weak to generalize and steroids are not routinely recommended. Corticosteroids are themselves a risk factor for tuberculous peritonitis.

nodes.description: Standard regimen as for pulmonary tuberculosis: isoniazid, rifampicin, pyrazinamide and ethambutol for two months, then isoniazid and rifampicin for at least four months. Randomized trials in intestinal and peritoneal tuberculosis found six months no worse than nine. The continuation phase is extended to seven months in HIV-positive patients not on antiretroviral therapy or responding slowly. Hepatotoxicity is the commonest reason to stop treatment and is more frequent with underlying liver disease, for which modified regimens are used.
